text: An inline table-valued function is locked to a single SELECT. Sometimes that's not enough — sometimes the logic genuinely needs more than one statement. That's what a multi-statement table-valued function is for.

Create function dbo dot ProductPriceHistory, returns at Result table, with its own column list — ProductID, ListPrice, PriceTier. Then a real BEGIN/END body: an INSERT into that table variable, computing a price tier with CASE, filtered to one product. It ends with a bare RETURN.

From the outside, calling it looks exactly like calling an inline function — SELECT star from dbo dot ProductPriceHistory of 680. The difference is entirely inside the function, not in how you use it.

That BEGIN/END body is why you'd reach for this. It can run multiple INSERT statements building the result in stages, use loops, branch differently depending on the parameter, even lean on temp tables — none of which a single SELECT can express.

But there's a real cost. SQL Server can't see inside that procedural body the way it can see through an inline function's single SELECT. Historically, that's meant the optimizer has to guess the row count coming out — often a poor, fixed guess — and a bad row estimate can lead to a bad join plan for everything downstream. An inline function doesn't have this problem, because there's nothing to guess.

So the rule of thumb: prefer an inline table-valued function whenever one SELECT can do the job, and reach for a multi-statement one only when the logic truly needs it. Next lesson moves from functions to triggers — code that runs automatically when a table changes.
